thread.title: BlackBerry (BB) 2nd Quarter Earnings: What to Expect

author: Richard Saintvilus
title: BlackBerry (BB) 2nd Quarter Earnings: What to Expect
text:
Shutterstock photo
Is BlackBerry ( BB ) still worth the wait?
The Canadian company, which has conceded the mobile hardware market to Apple ( AAPL ) and Samsung ( SSNLF ), has turned itself into a software and services specialist, focusing on enterprise applications, security and internet-of-things. But revenue growth has been hard to come by. And the company’s stock, which has fallen 8% year to date, reflects the impatient stance investors have taken.
The company is set to report second quarter fiscal 2019 earnings results before the opening bell Friday. With two straight earnings beats and counting, BlackBerry — owner of over 44,000 registered patents — must figure out a ways to get the top line growing again. Just as important, the company must also answer the question of whether it can grow its customer base while churning out recurring revenue streams in the next few years.
For the quarter that ended August, analysts expect BlackBerry to earn 1 cent per share on revenue of $209.38 million. This compares to the year-ago quarter when earnings came to 5 cents per share on revenue of $249 million. For the full year, ending in February, earnings are projected to be 9 cents per share, down from 14 cents a year ago, while revenue of $892.27 million would decline 7.7% year over year.
In the first quarter, BlackBerry easily surpassed Street earnings estimates by 100%. Despite the impressive beat, the stock tumbled some 10%. This has been a trend, which began in the fourth quarter when shares plunged 15% despite a beat. It begs the question of whether the stock will take another beating this quarter? Given that EPS expectations of 1-cent per is so low, which BlackBerry can easily exceed.
Investors instead continue to focus on the top line, which continues a gradual decline, albeit not as drastic as in previous years. On the bright side, however, the company’s Software & Services business, which in 2016 accounted for just 24% of total revenue, now accounts for 81% of its total revenue as of the end of fiscal 2018. And that number has grown from 50% in 2017.
The company believes it has an enormous opportunity to services customers in need of device security as the number of connected IoT devices grow over the next several years. BlackBerry estimates the number of connected devices to surge more than 600% in the next three years, rising from 6.4 billion connected devices in 2017 to 46 billion by the end of 2021
In other words, while Blackberry still has a long way to go to earn Wall Street’s trust, the company still has a massive opportunity to do it. What’s more, unlike previous years, BlackBerry — thanks to $2.4 billion in cash on the balance sheet — is better capitalized with the financial firepower to turn things around.
